To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of progression and death from prostate cancer is low for most patients with a rising prostate specific antigen level after radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy.

the risk of progression and mortality is higher in men with higher PSA doubling time, higher Gleason score, and shorter time from definitive therapy to rising PSA, and that these variables can be used to stratify patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups.

men with a rising PSA after definitive local therapy can be stratified into 2 risk groups based on the presence or absence of adverse pathologic features, and that men with no adverse pathologic features have a favorable prognosis, whereas those men with adverse pathologic features are at high risk for progression and mortality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods of cancer treatment.
the natural history of patients with a PSA relapse after definitive local therapy and with the identification of predictive variables for disease progression.
the development and evaluation of new technologies for prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
patients with a rising post-treatment PSA are at increased risk of death, but the absolute magnitude of the risk is unknown.
the majority of patients with a biochemical recurrence after local therapy for prostate carcinoma will have no clinical progression and will not die of prostate cancer.
there is no conclusive evidence for the best management of these men.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the natural history of patients with rising PSA after local therapy for prostate carcinoma has been better characterized and that there are now several useful predictive models that can be applied to this population.

the natural history of this group of men is variable, and that the best way to understand it is to continue to collect and analyze data in this group, and to develop and implement clinical trials to better define the best management options for these men.
patients with a rising prostate specific antigen (PSA), after definitive therapy for prostate cancer, have an unpredictable course and a variable prognosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the majority of men with rising PSA levels after local therapy are asymptomatic, have no evidence of distant disease on imaging and bone scans, have no clinical evidence of metastatic disease, and have a median survival that is comparable with that of men with a similar stage of disease who were initially treated with radical prostatectomy.
the natural history of men with a rising PSA after definitive local therapy is heterogeneous and complex.
there is no single model or set of variables that can accurately predict the clinical course of men with a rising PSA after definitive local therapy.
